Jane Eyre. Charlotte Brontë's novel about an orphaned governess who falls in love with her employer and confronts a dark secret that reframes her entire narrative.

Jane Eyre is an orphaned and impoverished young woman trained as a governess. She takes a position at Thornfield Hall in Yorkshire, where she becomes emotionally intimate with her employer, Edward Rochester. He is wealthy but mysterious, haunted by an unnamed past. Rochester proposes marriage. Jane accepts, believing she has finally found love and security after years of hardship. Plans proceed for the wedding ceremony.

But the ceremony is interrupted by a man named Mason, who reveals that Rochester is already married. His wife, Bertha Mason, lives in a locked room in the attic. She is portrayed as violent and deranged, prone to fire-setting and dangerous rages. Her confinement is presented as necessary for everyone's safety.

The twist destabilizes the romantic narrative. Rochester deceived Jane about his past. The secret wife is not merely a past relationship but a hidden person confined against her will. Jane eventually learns a far more troubling truth: Bertha is not merely mad but a victim of Rochester's control and isolation. Modern critical readings suggest Bertha's rage is justified resistance against her imprisonment.

Charlotte Brontë's novel is a foundational work of female agency in literature, yet it also grapples with the precarity of women's legal position within marriage and reflects attitudes toward colonialism and the silencing of marginalized voices. The gothic machinery of the attic imprisonment and hidden wife drives the psychological suspense that defines the novel's power.
